meaning: 1) Draws a natural conclusion from the preceding facts or information: "no wonder ...", "that means ...", "of course ..."; 2) restates or sums up: "in other words ..."; 3) the negative 〜わけではない expresses partial negation: "it's not that ...", "it doesn't (necessarily) mean ...".
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + わけだ; na-adjective stem + な・である + わけだ; noun + の・である + わけだ
usage: わけ is a formal noun preceded by noun-modifying forms: 行くわけだ, 高いわけだ, 静かなわけだ, 学生なわけだ (with nouns you can also say 学生というわけだ).
The polite form is 〜わけです; it often pairs with 「だから」, 「それで」, 「道理で」, or 「つまり」 to draw a result from a cause or to rephrase.
The negative 〜わけではない／〜わけじゃない doesn't negate the content itself but the conclusion that might be drawn from it: "it's not that ...". Adding も, as in 〜わけでもない, makes it softer.
「というわけで」 and 「そういうわけで」 at the start of a sentence or paragraph mean "so, and that's why", summing up what came before.
Distinguish it from 〜わけがない (impossible) and 〜わけにはいかない (can't do that): all three contain わけ, but their meanings are completely different.
scenarios: Suddenly understanding after hearing the reason (conversation): on learning that someone lived in America for ten years, 「えっ、10年もアメリカにいたの？」 followed by "no wonder their English is so good" with 〜わけだ.
Drawing a conclusion from data in explanatory texts or reports (written): 「つまり、人口は10年で2割減ったわけである。」
Politely denying the other person's assumption: 「料理が嫌いなわけじゃないけど、時間がないんです。」
Summing up and moving on: 「というわけで、来週の会議は中止になりました。」
etymology: わけ is written 「訳」 and is generally thought to be the nominalized continuative form of the verb 「分く／分ける」 (to divide), originally meaning "distinction, discernment", and by extension "logic, reason, cause". The kanji 「訳」 ("explain, translate") was borrowed to write it. Formal noun わけ + copula だ literally means "(this) stands to reason, that's how it is", which gives rise to the "naturally" and "in other words" uses.
examples: He lived in Japan for three years, so no wonder his Japanese is good.
If you study two hours a day, that means you study fourteen hours a week.
It's not that I dislike meat; I just don't eat much of it.
So, tomorrow's game has been postponed.

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: 〜わけがない means "there's no way ...", a strong denial of possibility; 〜わけではない is only a partial denial, "it's not that ...". 「高いわけがない」 = it can't possibly be expensive; 「高いわけではない」 = it's not exactly expensive (but not cheap either).

similar.title: 〜わけにはいかない
similar.explanation: Means "can't (do that)" for reasons of logic, obligation, or social norms; it is about an action being unacceptable, not an inference. 「休むわけにはいかない」 = I can't take the day off.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 〜はずだ is a prediction or inference based on grounds (should be ...), with the conclusion not yet confirmed; 〜わけだ is mostly used when the facts are already clear and the speaker accepts and understands the reason. 「彼は来るはずだ」 is a prediction; 「だから来たわけだ」 is understanding.

similar.title: 〜ということだ
similar.explanation: Can also mean "in other words", but it is a more objective, written rephrasing and also has a hearsay use; 〜わけだ carries a subjective sense of "I see, that makes sense".

meaning: 1) Verb dictionary form + わけにはいかない: for reasons of logic, responsibility, obligation, or social norms, "can't (do) ...", "it wouldn't be right to ..."; 2) verb nai-form + わけにはいかない: "can't not ...", "have to ...", i.e. one is morally or socially obliged to do it.
connection: Verb dictionary form + わけにはいかない; verb nai-form + ないわけにはいかない
usage: It's not about lacking the ability (that's 〜できない), but "although I could, it's not acceptable morally, given my position, or by the rules".
Past 〜わけにはいかなかった; polite 〜わけにはいきません; in speech は can be dropped: 〜わけにいかない; in writing 〜わけにはいかず.
「〜ないわけにはいかない」 is a double negative meaning "I really have to, morally"; compared with 〜なければならない it puts more stress on external pressure or personal obligations.
It can be strengthened with も: 「黙って見ているわけにもいかない」 (I can't just stand by and watch either).
The subject is usually the speaker, explaining their own position; for a third person it is mostly the speaker's guess about their situation.
scenarios: Explaining at work why you can't act freely: 「明日は大事な会議があるので、休むわけにはいかない。」
Politely declining someone's kindness (conversation): 「お気持ちはうれしいですが、そんな高いものをいただくわけにはいきません。」
Having to do something out of obligation: 「先生に頼まれたら、引き受けないわけにはいかない。」
Describing a character's inner struggle in novels and essays: 「ここで諦めるわけにはいかなかった。」
etymology: わけ（訳） originally means "reason, logic", and いく（行く） in the negative いかない means "doesn't work out, can't be done" (as in 「うまくいかない」). Together they literally mean "it doesn't work in terms of reason", i.e. "it's not right to do so". は is a contrastive particle that strengthens the negation.
examples: I have an exam tomorrow, so I can't go out and have fun.
I came by car, so I can't drink.
If the department manager asks, I can't very well refuse.
It's my friend's wedding, so I can't not go.

similar.title: 〜わけだ／〜わけではない
similar.explanation: 〜わけだ expresses an inference, "no wonder, that means"; 〜わけではない is a partial negation, "it's not that". Both differ from 〜わけにはいかない ("can't do"); watch for the presence of には.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Expresses a general obligation or necessity; 〜ないわけにはいかない stresses "I have no choice but to, because of obligations or my position", with a sense of resignation.

similar.title: 〜ことはできない
similar.explanation: Simply means it is impossible or not allowed, more objectively; 〜わけにはいかない focuses on the speaker's own moral judgment and situation.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: "Have no choice but to", stressing being forced by circumstances to act against one's will; more written. 〜ないわけにはいかない is more about social or personal obligation and is used in both speech and writing.

meaning: 1) The speaker (subject) makes a decision of their own will: "decide to ..."; 2) 〜ことにしている: a habit or rule resulting from a decision: "make it a rule to ...", "always make a point of ..."; 3) 〜ことにする can also mean "treat it as ..., pretend that ...".
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことにする (past: ことにした; habit: ことにしている)
usage: 「ことにした」 expresses a decision just made and is the most common; 「ことにする」 expresses a decision made on the spot or not yet carried out.
「ことにしている」 expresses a rule you set for yourself or a long-standing habit: 「毎朝走ることにしている」.
Negative decisions use the nai-form: 「もうタバコを吸わないことにした。」
After the past tense, as in 「聞かなかったことにする」 or 「なかったことにする」, it means "pretend I didn't hear it / pretend it never happened".
Polite: ことにします／ことにしました／ことにしています.
scenarios: Announcing your decision to others (conversation): 「来年、日本に留学することにしました。」
Describing personal habits or health rules: 「夜9時以降は何も食べないことにしています。」
Explaining an internal company decision in business (mostly one's own decision): 「今回は見送ることにいたしました。」
Treating something as if it never happened: 「今の話は聞かなかったことにします。」
etymology: こと（事） is a formal noun that nominalizes the preceding action; に marks the result or choice; する means the subject acts deliberately. Literally, "to make (something) one's choice", hence the emphasis on the subject's own decision. By contrast, なる expresses a natural change, giving 〜ことになる (a result or decision formed externally).
examples: I've decided to go jogging every morning starting next month.
For my health, I make it a rule not to drink coffee at night.
After thinking it over carefully, I decided to take the job.
Let's pretend we didn't hear what was just said.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: 〜ことになる means the decision was made by an organization, others, or circumstances, and the speaker isn't the one actively deciding; 〜ことにする is the subject's own decision. Even for your own decision, ことになりました sounds more modest and objective.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 〜つもりだ expresses an intention in your mind, not necessarily a firm decision; 〜ことにした means the decision has been made.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: Expresses an intention, "I'm thinking of ..."; less certain than a decision, still at the considering stage.

similar.title: Noun + にする
similar.explanation: 「コーヒーにする」 means choosing a noun among several options (I'll have coffee) and follows nouns; 〜ことにする follows verbs and means deciding to do something.

meaning: 1) A decision, arrangement, or outcome not of the speaker's own will: "it has been decided that ...", "it's been arranged that ..."; 2) 〜ことになっている: rules, customs, or schedules: "is supposed to ...", "according to the rules / plan ..."; 3) a logically calculated result: "that means ...", "(this way) you'll end up ...".
connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + ことになる (past: ことになった; rules: ことになっている)
usage: 「ことになった」 is the most common, describing things decided by a company, school, other people, or circumstances.
Even for something you decided yourself, 〜ことになりました avoids stressing your personal will and sounds modest and objective; it's common in formal announcements and greetings.
「〜ことになっている」 expresses rules, laws, customs, or fixed schedules: 「ここではタバコを吸ってはいけないことになっている。」
Used for calculations or rephrasing: 「このままだと遅刻することになる」 (at this rate we'll be late).
Polite: ことになります／ことになりました／ことになっています.
scenarios: Job transfers and personnel announcements (formal): 「4月から大阪支社に転勤することになりました。」
Explaining rules: 「授業中は携帯電話の電源を切ることになっています。」
Announcing a schedule: 「会議は来週の月曜日に行うことになった。」
Calculating consequences or warning someone: 「今やめたら、今までの努力が無駄になることになるよ。」
etymology: こと（事） is a formal noun, に marks the result of a change, and なる means "to come about, to become". Literally, "things have become the state of ...". Because なる doesn't highlight an agent, it expresses that the decision was formed outside the speaker's will, and Japanese speakers often use it to sound modest and avoid seeming self-assertive.
examples: I'll be working at the head office in Tokyo from next year.
In this dormitory, you're supposed to be back by 10 p.m.
It's been decided that the meeting will be canceled.
If you spend 1,000 yen a day, that means you spend 30,000 yen a month.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: Stresses the subject's own decision; 〜ことになる stresses that the decision was formed externally or the result came about naturally.

similar.title: 〜ようになる
similar.explanation: Expresses a gradual change in ability, habit, or state (come to be able to ...), not a decision; 〜ことになる is about decisions and arrangements. 「話せるようになった」 and 「話すことになった」 mean completely different things.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: In the sense of a calculated result they are similar, but 〜わけだ leans toward accepting something as natural ("no wonder"), while 〜ことになる leans toward "by calculation, this is the result".

meaning: 1) Cause: "due to ..., because of ..."; 2) means or method: "by means of ..., through ..."; 3) in passive sentences, the agent (creator, discoverer, etc.): "by ..."; 4) variation: "depending on ..., (differs) by ..."; 5) 〜によると／〜によれば: source of information, "according to ...".
connection: Noun + によって／により／による + noun／によっては／によると・によれば
usage: To link clauses, use によって (spoken or written) or により (more written, common in news); to modify a noun, use 「による + noun」, as in 「地震による被害」.
In passive sentences, the agent of creation, invention, discovery, etc. must be marked with によって, not に: 「この小説は夏目漱石によって書かれた。」
「〜によって違う／異なる／さまざまだ」 means "differs depending on ..."; 「〜によっては」 means "in some ... (it may even ...)", highlighting certain cases.
「〜によると／〜によれば」 gives the source of information and often pairs with そうだ・らしい at the end of the sentence.
The causal use is mostly for objective descriptions of accidents, disasters, etc., and is not suitable for giving reasons for personal requests or commands.
scenarios: News reports on the causes of disasters (written): 「台風による大雨で、電車が止まった。」
Explanatory texts naming the creator of an invention or work: 「電話はベルによって発明された。」
Explaining differences: 「習慣は国によって違います。」
Relaying information: 「天気予報によると、明日は雪が降るそうだ。」
etymology: よる is written 「因る・依る・拠る・由る」, originally meaning "to rely on, to depend on, to be based on". In the old form 「によりて」, より (continuative form) + て underwent a geminate sound change, giving modern 「によって」; the continuative 「により」 keeps the suspended-clause use and sounds more literary. Each kanji has its own focus: 因る = cause, 依る = relying on a means, 拠る = basis, 由る = origin.
examples: This temple was built about a thousand years ago and has been protected by many people ever since.
The damage caused by the earthquake was greater than expected.
Ways of thinking differ from person to person.
According to the news, train fares will go up from next month.
Through hard work, I achieved success.

similar.title: 〜おかげで
similar.explanation: Also expresses a cause, but with gratitude, for good results; 〜によって is a neutral, objective cause, mostly used in writing.

similar.title: 〜せいで
similar.explanation: Expresses the cause of a bad result, with a tone of blame; 〜によって has no emotional coloring.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: Means "based on ...", stressing the content of the basis; the "basis" sense of 〜によって is weaker, and it more often expresses means or cause.

similar.title: 〜で
similar.explanation: The case particle で can also express means or cause (バスで行く, 病気で休む), simply and colloquially; 〜によって is more formal and written.

meaning: Indicates the topic or content of talking, thinking, investigating, explaining, etc.: "about ..., concerning ..., on ...".
connection: Noun + について／についての + noun／については／についても (formal: につきまして)
usage: Usually followed by verbs related to language, thought, or research, such as 話す, 説明する, 調べる, 考える, 書く, 聞く.
To modify a noun use 「についての + noun」: 「日本の文化についての本」.
Add は for a topic or contrast: 「この点については後で説明します」; add も: 「〜についても」.
In very formal situations (business, speeches), use 「につきまして」: 「この件につきましては、改めてご連絡いたします。」
Distinguish it from the te-form of the verbs 「着く・就く」, as in 「席について」 (take a seat) or 「身について」 (be learned, become second nature); these are not this grammar point.
scenarios: Classes, reports, and papers (written or spoken): 「日本の環境問題についてレポートを書いた。」
Raising an agenda item in a meeting or discussion: 「次に、予算について話し合いましょう。」
Asking for information or advice: 「この言葉の意味について教えてください。」
Formal phrasing in business emails: 「お問い合わせの件につきまして、ご回答いたします。」
etymology: It comes from the verb 「就く（つく）」, originally meaning "to attach to, to approach, to follow". The old form 「に就きて」 became 「に就いて」 through i-onbin and was then written in kana as 「について」, meaning "attaching to ... (to talk)", i.e. "around ..., about ...". The continuative 「につき」 still appears in written language as 「〜につき」 (concerning / due to / per ...).
examples: I'm researching Japanese history.
I'd like to hear everyone's opinions on this issue.
I read a book about the environment.
As for the details, the person in charge will explain them to you.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: 〜に対して marks the target an action or emotion is directed at (toward ...), as in 「親に対して失礼だ」; 〜について marks the topic being discussed. 「先生について話す」 = talk about the teacher; 「先生に対して話す」 = talk to the teacher.

similar.title: 〜に関して
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning as 〜について, but more written and formal, and slightly broader in scope ("regarding ...").

similar.title: 〜をめぐって
similar.explanation: Means "over ..., surrounding ... (a dispute or conflict)", mostly used when several opinions clash; 〜について has no such nuance.

meaning: 1) The target of an action, attitude, or emotion: "toward ..., to ..."; 2) contrast: "in contrast to ..., whereas ..."; 3) ratio: "per ..., for every ..." (as in 「学生1人に対して」).
connection: Noun + に対して／に対し／に対しては／に対しても／に対する + noun; contrastive use: plain form + の + に対して
usage: In the "target" use it is usually followed by words expressing attitudes, reactions, or actions: 反対する, 抗議する, 親切だ, 厳しい, 興味を持つ, etc.
To modify a noun use 「に対する + noun」 or 「に対しての + noun」: 「お客様に対する態度」.
In the contrastive use after a clause, add の: 「兄が背が高いのに対して、弟は低い。」
「に対し」 is the written suspended form, common in news and papers.
Ratio use: 「学生20人に対して先生が1人」 (one teacher for every twenty students).
scenarios: Describing attitudes or manners: 「目上の人に対して、そんな言い方は失礼だ。」
Making contrasts in papers or reports (written): 「都市部の人口が増えているのに対し、農村部は減少している。」
Expressing ratios or rates: 「応募者100人に対して合格者は5人だった。」
Responding to inquiries or complaints: 「お客様からの苦情に対して、すぐに対応した。」
etymology: 「対する（たいする）」 is a suru-verb formed from the Sino-Japanese element 「対」 (on'yomi たい, "facing, opposite") plus する, originally meaning "to face, to be opposite, to oppose". に marks the target, and the te-form links to the following clause. The suspended form 「に対し」 and the attributive form 「に対する」 both come from the conjugation of this suru-verb and have the written flavor of the kanbun-reading style.
examples: The teacher is very kind to the students.
Many people opposed that opinion.
Whereas the older brother is cheerful, the younger one is quiet.
Please be careful about the language you use with customers.

similar.title: 〜について
similar.explanation: 〜について marks the topic being discussed or studied (about); 〜に対して marks the direct target of an attitude or action (toward).

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: 〜にとって evaluates something from someone's standpoint (for ..., to ...), usually followed by evaluations like 大切だ or 難しい; 〜に対して is followed by attitudes and actions. 「私にとって大切だ」 cannot be said as 「私に対して大切だ」.

similar.title: 〜に反して
similar.explanation: Means "contrary to (expectations, wishes)", as in 「予想に反して」; the contrastive use of 〜に対して simply compares two things side by side, without the sense of "going against".

meaning: Indicates identity, qualification, position, capacity, or category: "as ..., in the capacity of ..."; 〜としては means "from the standpoint of ...", and 〜としても means "even as ...".
connection: Noun + として／としては／としても／としての + noun
usage: It follows nouns expressing identity, position, qualification, purpose, or category: 「留学生として」, 「代表として」, 「趣味として」.
To modify a noun use 「としての + noun」: 「教師としての責任」.
「〜としては」 gives a judgment from a certain standpoint: 「私としては、この案に賛成です」; it can also mean "(surprisingly) for a ...": 「子供としては背が高い」 (tall for a child).
Don't confuse it with volitional form + とする (「出かけようとした」 = was about to go out), adverb + として (「ほっとして」, 「じっとして」), or 「落として」; these are not this grammar point.
「〜をはじめとして」 (starting with ...), 「主として」 (mainly), 「依然として」 (still) are set expressions.
scenarios: Introducing yourself or explaining your status: 「交換留学生として日本に来ました。」
Stating a position in business or public settings: 「会社としては、この問題に責任を持って対応します。」
Explaining a use or category: 「この部屋は会議室として使われている。」
Discussing responsibilities and roles in commentary or essays: 「親としての役割を考える。」
etymology: Made of the case particle 「と」, which marks content or result, and 「して」, the te-form of the verb 「する」; it shares its origin with 「AをBとする」 (to treat A as B, to regard A as B). In the traditional Japanese reading of Classical Chinese texts (kanbun kundoku), 「〜として」 was often used to render expressions meaning "taking ... as" or "being ...", which gave it the sense "in the capacity of ...", and it gradually became fixed as a compound particle.
examples: As a doctor, he has saved many lives.
This building is used as a library.
Personally, I agree with that opinion.
I feel my responsibility as a teacher.

similar.title: 〜にとって
similar.explanation: 〜にとって expresses an evaluative standpoint, "for ..., to ...", followed by evaluations (大切だ, 難しい); 〜として expresses identity or capacity, followed by actions or judgments. 「親として反対だ」 (I object as a parent) vs. 「親にとって嬉しい」 (it makes parents happy).

similar.title: 〜の立場で
similar.explanation: Also means taking a certain standpoint but stresses the "position" more concretely; 〜として is more concise and general.

similar.title: 〜としたら・〜とすると
similar.explanation: Express a hypothesis, "if ..."; they are conditional forms of とする and differ in meaning from 〜として, which expresses capacity.

meaning: 1) Purpose: "in order to ..., for ..."; 2) cause or reason: "because of ..., due to ..." (fairly formal); 3) benefit: "for the sake of (someone)".
connection: Purpose: verb dictionary form / noun + の + ために; cause: plain form of verbs and adjectives (often past) / na-adjective + な / noun + の + ために
usage: For purpose, both clauses share the same subject and the first must be a deliberate action (volitional verb): 「家を買うために貯金する」. With non-volitional or potential verbs, use 〜ように for purpose.
For cause, the first clause is usually past tense or a state, and the second is usually an uncontrollable result: 「雨が降ったために、試合が中止になった」; formal and written in tone.
Nouns need の: 「健康のために」, 「家族のために」. To modify a noun use 「〜ための + noun」.
The causal use can be written 「〜ため、」 without に, common in notices and news: 「工事のため、通行止めです。」
「〜のためになる」 means "to be good for ..., beneficial to ...".
scenarios: Explaining your goals (conversation, essays): 「日本の大学に入るために、毎日勉強しています。」
Giving reasons in public notices (written): 「台風のため、本日の営業は中止いたします。」
Doing something for someone else: 「子どものために、毎朝お弁当を作る。」
Explaining means and ends in argumentative writing, e.g. 「環境を守るための取り組み」 (efforts to protect the environment).
etymology: ため was originally a noun that already had the meanings "benefit, advantage", "purpose", and "reason, cause" in Classical Japanese. In the traditional Japanese reading of Classical Chinese texts, 「〜のために」 was regularly used to render a Chinese preposition meaning both "for (the sake of)" and "because of", so it came to cover both purpose and cause, as it still does today.
examples: I'm saving money from my part-time job in order to study abroad.
I walk every day for my health.
Because of the heavy rain, the train was delayed.
This is a book for children.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: 〜ように follows non-volitional verbs, potential verbs, or negatives (聞こえるように, 忘れないように), and the two clauses can have different subjects; 〜ために follows volitional verbs, and the subjects are the same.

similar.title: 〜から
similar.explanation: The most common way to give a reason in speech; it can be followed by commands, requests, and other subjective content. The causal 〜ために is more written and objective, and its second clause is usually an established fact.

similar.title: 〜おかげで
similar.explanation: A cause with a tone of gratitude, used for good results; 〜ために is neutral.

similar.title: 〜には
similar.explanation: 「〜するには」 means "in order to ... (you need ...)", followed by a necessary condition or evaluation; 〜ために is followed by the concrete action taken for the purpose.

meaning: Expresses taking an action in order to achieve a certain state or result: "so that (one can) ...", "in order to be able to ...", "so as not to ...". At the end of a sentence, 〜ますように can also express a wish or prayer: "I hope ..., may ...".
connection: Verb dictionary form (mostly non-volitional or potential verbs) / verb nai-form + ように
usage: The first clause usually has a non-volitional verb (見える, 聞こえる, 治る), a potential verb (話せる, 読める), or a negative (忘れない, 遅れない), expressing the desired state.
The subjects of the two clauses can differ: 「後ろの人にも聞こえるように、大きな声で話す」 (I speak loudly so that the people at the back can hear too).
Unlike 〜ために, 〜ように generally doesn't follow the dictionary form of a volitional verb; "in order to buy" is 「買うために」, but "so that I can buy" can be 「買えるように」.
Sentence-final 「〜ますように」 expresses a wish or prayer: 「合格できますように。」
Distinguish it from 〜ようになる (change), 〜ようにする (making an effort), and noun + のように (simile); those are not part of this entry.
scenarios: Reminding or advising others (conversation): 「風邪をひかないように、暖かくしてね。」
Explaining your own preparations: 「忘れないように、手帳に書いておきます。」
Explaining the purpose of a procedure in teaching or manuals: 「誰でも読めるように、ふりがなをつけました。」
Wishes and prayers, on ema plaques or greeting cards: 「みんなが幸せになりますように。」
etymology: よう is written 「様」; it comes from やう, the go-on reading of the kanji 様, which later changed to よう, and originally meant "appearance, state, manner". 「〜ように」 literally means "(aiming) to become the state of ...", which gives the purpose use; the same 「様」 also gave rise to a whole family of grammar, including simile (〜のように) and change (〜ようになる).
examples: I'll write it down so I don't forget.
I wrote the characters large so that the people at the back could see them well.
I left home early so as not to miss the train.
I practice every day so that I can speak Japanese well.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: 〜ために follows volitional verbs, and both clauses share a subject; 〜ように follows non-volitional verbs, potential verbs, or negatives, and the subjects can differ.

similar.title: 〜ようにする
similar.explanation: Expresses making an effort or taking care to do something (try to ...), with する directly after ように; the purpose 〜ように is followed by a concrete action.

similar.title: 〜ようになる
similar.explanation: Expresses a change in ability or habit (come to be able to ...), with なる directly after ように.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜のように
similar.explanation: 「雪のように白い」 is a simile, "like ...", preceded by noun + の; different from the purpose 〜ように.

meaning: 1) Gives an extreme example, implying that everything else goes without saying: "even ..."; 2) 〜さえ〜ば: the one and only necessary condition: "as long as ..., if only ...".
connection: Noun (+ particle) + さえ; noun + でさえ; verb continuative form + さえ + すれば; noun + さえ + あれば
usage: After subjects and objects it directly replaces が・を: 「子どもさえ知っている」, 「水さえ飲めない」; other particles remain: 「家族にさえ言わなかった」.
After subjects 「でさえ」 is common: 「専門家でさえわからない」.
The 「〜さえ〜ば」 pattern: noun + さえ + あれば／なければ; verb masu-stem + さえ + すれば; te-form + さえいれば: 「薬を飲みさえすれば治る」.
In the "even" sense, the second clause is usually negative or surprising; 「〜さえ〜ば」 stresses "just meet this one condition and nothing else is a problem".
Distinguish it from the さえ inside verbs such as 「押さえる」, 「支える」, 「遮る」, and 「さえずる」.
scenarios: Emphasizing something surprising or extreme (conversation, novels): 「忙しくて、ご飯を食べる時間さえない。」
Describing a lack of ability: 「ひらがなさえ読めなかった。」
Encouraging someone by stressing the one condition: 「やる気さえあれば、誰でもできる。」
Advertisements and manuals: 「このボタンを押しさえすれば、自動で動きます。」
etymology: Modern さえ comes from the old adverbial particle 「さへ」, which in the Heian period mainly expressed "addition" (on top of that, ... too). さへ is generally thought to derive from the verb 「添ふ（そふ）」 (to add, to accompany). In Classical Japanese, giving an extreme example was originally mainly the job of 「だに」 and 「すら」; さへ gradually absorbed these uses and became the modern "even". The conditional use 「〜さえ〜ば」 also developed from the early modern period onward.
examples: I'm so busy I don't even have time to eat lunch.
Even experts don't know the cause.
I used to think that as long as I had money, I could do anything.
As long as you take this medicine, you'll get better right away.

similar.title: 〜も
similar.explanation: 「子どもも知っている」 just means "also", without the extreme emphasis of "even"; 〜さえ stresses a surprising degree.

similar.title: 〜まで
similar.explanation: 「〜まで」 can also mean "even", but it is mostly used in affirmative sentences to stress that the scope extends to something surprising (「先生まで笑った」); 〜さえ is mostly used with negatives or in the "as long as" condition.

similar.title: 〜すら
similar.explanation: Same meaning as さえ in the "even" sense, but more written and stronger, and it has no conditional 「〜すら〜ば」 use.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: Expresses addition, "not only ... but also ..."; 〜さえ gives an extreme example without needing to mention another item.

meaning: Expresses addition: "not only ... but also ...", "not just ..., ... as well". Often paired with 「〜も」 or 「〜まで」 in the second clause.
connection: Noun + ばかりでなく; plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + ばかりでなく; na-adjective + な + ばかりでなく
usage: Typical pattern: 「AばかりでなくBも〜」, where B is usually something of a higher degree or broader scope than A.
In speech you can say 「〜ばかりじゃなく」; adding は, as in 「〜ばかりではなく」, sounds more formal.
The second clause can be a command, request, invitation, or other volitional expression: 「漢字ばかりでなく、文法も勉強しなさい」; this differs from 〜ばかりか.
The near-synonym 「〜だけでなく」 is more colloquial and more widely used; 〜ばかりでなく is slightly more written.
Distinguish it from 「〜たばかり」 (have just ...).
scenarios: Describing someone's or something's many strengths: 「彼は勉強ばかりでなく、スポーツも得意だ。」
Stating the scope of an impact in news or explanatory writing (written): 「この問題は日本ばかりでなく、世界中で起きている。」
A teacher giving students advice: 「教科書ばかりでなく、新聞も読んでみてください。」
etymology: ばかり is generally thought to come from 「はかり」, the noun form of the verb 「計る・量る（はかる）」 (to measure), with voicing; it originally meant "extent, approximate amount" and later became a limiting adverbial particle meaning "only, just". 「ばかりでなく」 thus means "not only (these)", expressing addition by negating a limitation.
examples: He can speak not only English but also Chinese.
This shop is not only cheap, but the food is good too.
Not just children but adults too are hooked on this anime.
Don't just study; get some exercise once in a while too.

similar.title: 〜ばかりか
similar.explanation: Same meaning, but 〜ばかりか carries the speaker's surprise or strong feeling, the second clause is often something more extreme, and it cannot be followed by commands, requests, or other volitional expressions.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning; more colloquial and the most common. 〜ばかりでなく is slightly more written.

similar.title: 〜うえに
similar.explanation: Means "moreover, on top of that", adding items in the same direction; not followed by commands or invitations.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: Means an action has just been completed (have just ...); unrelated to ばかりでなく ("not only").

meaning: Expresses a very confident inference by the speaker based on some grounds: "must be ..., surely ..., there's no doubt that ...".
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + に違いない; na-adjective stem / noun + に違いない (without だ)
usage: Nouns and na-adjectives attach directly, without だ: 「犯人は彼に違いない」, 「静かに違いない」.
Confidence is very high, but it is still an inference, not a statement of fact; more certain than 〜だろう or 〜かもしれない.
Polite: 「〜に違いありません」; past: 「〜に違いなかった」.
Somewhat written; common in reasoning passages in novels and essays. In conversation, 「きっと〜と思う」 or 「〜に決まっている」 are more common.
Often used with きっと: 「きっと疲れているに違いない。」
scenarios: Mystery novels and detective scenes (written): 「犯人はこの部屋にいた人に違いない。」
Inferring someone's situation from signs: 「電気がついているから、彼はまだ会社にいるに違いない。」
Expressing strong conviction or looking back on the past: 「あの時、母は寂しかったに違いない。」
etymology: 「違い（ちがい）」 is the nominalized continuative form of the verb 「違う」, meaning "error, difference". 「に違いない」 literally means "there is no mistake (on this point)", i.e. "it is certainly so". The more formal written 「に相違ない」 has exactly the same structure.
examples: She practiced so hard, so she's sure to pass.
The lights are on, so Mr. Tanaka must still be at home.
This handwriting must be a child's.
Seeing the surprise on his face, I thought something must have happened.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 〜はずだ is a "should" worked out from objective reasoning or facts; 〜に違いない is the speaker's strong subjective conviction (often based on intuition).

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Means "maybe, possibly", with a likelihood of about 50% or less; 〜に違いない is highly confident.

similar.title: 〜に決まっている
similar.explanation: Also means "surely, definitely", but is more colloquial and more subjectively assertive, often with a "goes without saying" tone.

meaning: Strongly denies a possibility based on reasoning, facts, or common sense: "there's no way ..., can't possibly ...".
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + はずがない; na-adjective + な + はずがない; noun + の + はずがない
usage: A negative inference with very high confidence, like "absolutely impossible". In speech が can be dropped as 「はずない」, and 「はずはない」 adds contrastive emphasis.
Polite: 「〜はずがありません」; past: 「〜はずがなかった」.
Difference from 〜ないはずだ: 〜ないはずだ is a weaker guess, "it shouldn't be ..."; 〜はずがない means "it simply can't be", a much stronger denial.
What is denied is often what the other person said or a rumor: 「そんなはずがない！」 (That can't be!).
Note that 「〜はずじゃなかった」 (it wasn't supposed to be like this) is the negative past of 〜はずだ and means something different.
scenarios: Strongly rejecting a rumor or someone's claim (conversation): 「彼がうそをつくはずがない。」
Judging by common sense: 「こんな簡単な問題、わからないはずがない。」
Exclaiming in surprise or disbelief: 「そんなはずはない！確かにここに置いたのに。」
etymology: はず is written 「筈」 and originally referred to the notch at the end of an arrow that fits onto the bowstring (矢筈). The notch and the string necessarily fit together, which extended to "it stands to reason, naturally so". 「はずがない」 thus means "there's no reason for that", i.e. it's simply impossible.
examples: Someone as kind as that couldn't possibly say something so cruel.
I locked it, so there's no way the door is open.
He practices every day, so there's no way he'll lose.
There's no way the first dish you ever made is going to taste good.

similar.title: 〜はずだ
similar.explanation: 〜はずだ is an affirmative inference, "should ..."; its negative 〜ないはずだ (shouldn't be) is weaker than 〜はずがない (can't possibly be).

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning as 〜はずがない; 〜わけがない is more colloquial and emotional, while 〜はずがない leans more on objective grounds.

similar.title: 〜に違いない
similar.explanation: A strong affirmative inference (must be ...), the exact opposite direction of 〜はずがない.

meaning: 1) After nouns: having the quality or tendency of ..., "...-ish, -like, seems like ..."; 2) after the verb continuative form: prone to ..., "tends to ..." (e.g. 忘れっぽい, 怒りっぽい); 3) in casual speech after a clause, a guess: "seems like ...".
connection: Noun + っぽい; verb masu-stem + っぽい; (colloquial) plain form + っぽい
usage: Conjugates as an i-adjective: っぽく, っぽかった, っぽくない, っぽさ.

After nouns it often carries a negative evaluation or a sense of "not what it should be": 「子どもっぽい」 (childish), 「安っぽい」 (cheap-looking); it can also neutrally describe colors or textures: 「白っぽい」 (whitish), 「水っぽい」 (watery).
After the verb continuative form it expresses personality tendencies: 「忘れっぽい」 (forgetful), 「飽きっぽい」 (easily bored), 「怒りっぽい」 (short-tempered).
In young people's speech it can follow a clause to express a guess: 「あの人、先生っぽいね」, 「雨が降るっぽい」 (quite casual; not suitable for formal situations).
Overall it is a strongly colloquial expression; formal writing tends to use 〜らしい, 〜のような, etc.
scenarios: Commenting on someone's personality or behavior (conversation among friends): 「彼は大人なのに、子どもっぽいところがある。」
Describing colors or appearance: 「白っぽいシャツを着た人。」
Complaining about your own bad habits: 「最近、忘れっぽくて困る。」
Casual guesses by young people: 「あの店、今日休みっぽいよ。」
etymology: 「っぽい」 is an adjective-forming suffix, generally thought to have formed by adding a geminate consonant before 「ぽい」; early examples include 「荒っぽい」, 「俗っぽい」, and 「水っぽい」. Its exact origin is disputed. In recent decades its range has kept expanding, and it can now attach freely to all kinds of nouns and even whole clauses, which is regarded as a colloquial, newer usage. (Compare English "-ish", which has similarly spread to casual uses like "sixish" or "I'm done-ish".)
examples: He's already 30, yet he keeps saying such childish things.
Lately I've become forgetful.
That whitish building is the station.
This bag looks a little cheap, doesn't it?

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: Noun + らしい means "having the typical, proper qualities of that thing", mostly positive: 「男らしい」 (manly); 〜っぽい means "somewhat like", often negative: 「男っぽい」 (mannish).

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Express simile or inference and are fairly neutral; 〜っぽい is more colloquial and leans toward "having a certain tendency or air".

similar.title: 〜がち
similar.explanation: Means "(something bad) tends to happen, happens often", as in 「病気がち」 or 「遅れがち」; 〜っぽい after verbs focuses on personality tendencies.

meaning: 1) Checking something you can't quite remember, with the listener or yourself: "what was ... again?", "... wasn't it?"; 2) reminiscing about the past: "back then, I used to ..., didn't I".
connection: Plain form (noun・na-adjective + だった／だ) + っけ; past form + っけ; polite 〜でしたっけ／〜ましたっけ
usage: Common forms: 「〜だっけ」, 「〜たっけ」, 「〜だったっけ」, 「〜でしたっけ」, 「〜ましたっけ」.
Mostly used at the end of a sentence with question intonation, and can combine with か・ね・な: 「何だったっけな」.
When talking to yourself it expresses reminiscence: 「子どものころ、よくここで遊んだっけ。」
It is colloquial and not used in formal writing; 「〜でしたっけ」 can be used with a boss, but it still sounds a bit casual.
Distinguish it from the っけ in words like 「あっけない」 and 「そっけない」.
scenarios: Can't remember and checking with a friend: 「あの人、名前何だっけ？」
Confirming a schedule with a coworker: 「会議は何時からでしたっけ？」
Reminiscing to yourself (novels, essays): 「昔はよく父と釣りに行ったっけ。」
etymology: It is generally thought to come from the Classical Japanese auxiliary 「けり」, which expressed recollection and exclamation. けり was later simplified to 「け」, and in colloquial speech a geminate was added to give 「っけ」. It kept the sense of "recalling the past" and further developed the use of checking a memory with the listener.
examples: Huh, what day is it today again?
What time did the last meeting start again?
When I was a kid, I often swam in this river.
Mr. Tanaka is from Osaka, isn't he?

similar.title: 〜か
similar.explanation: A plain question; 〜っけ is checking something you knew but can't recall.

similar.title: 〜よね
similar.explanation: Seeks confirmation of something you believe is correct, with some confidence; 〜っけ is checking when your memory is hazy.

similar.title: 〜たものだ
similar.explanation: Reminisces about things that happened repeatedly in the past, with strong feeling, and is more written; the reminiscing 〜っけ is more colloquial and personal.

meaning: Taking the opportunity of doing one thing to do another: "while you're at it ..., on the way ..., while ... anyway".
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + ついでに; noun + の + ついでに (as a standalone adverb: ついでに)
usage: The first clause is the main purpose; the second is the secondary thing done along the way.
The dictionary form means "while going to do ...", the ta-form "after doing ...": 「買い物に行くついでに」, 「駅まで来たついでに」.
Nouns take の, usually action nouns: 「散歩のついでに」, 「出張のついでに」.
It can stand alone as an adverb at the start of a sentence: 「ついでに、これもお願い。」 There is also 「ついでの時に」 (whenever it's convenient).
Distinguish it from the ついで in 「〜に次いで」 (second only to ...) and 「注いで」 (pouring).
scenarios: Asking someone to do something on the way (conversation): 「コンビニに行くついでに、牛乳を買ってきてくれない？」
Describing an itinerary: 「大阪に出張したついでに、京都にも寄った。」
Politely adding an extra request: 「ついでに、この書類もコピーしてもらえますか。」
etymology: 「ついで」 is written 「序で」. It comes from 「つぎ」, the continuative form of the verb 「次ぐ（つぐ）」 (to follow, to come next), plus 「て」, which became 「ついで」 through i-onbin. It originally meant "order, sequence", and extended to "an incidental opportunity, convenience". The kanji 「序」 itself also means "order".
examples: When you go to the post office, please mail this letter too.
I bought some bread while I was out for a walk.
While I was in Tokyo, I took the chance to see an old friend.
While I was at it, I cleaned the room too.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: Two actions happening simultaneously (while ...ing); 〜ついでに means using the chance of doing one thing to do another, not necessarily at the same time.

similar.title: 〜がてら
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, "while ..., also ...", but the first item is usually 散歩, 買い物, etc., it is more written, and both activities are equally intended.

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: Means "while ... (lasts)", stressing a time span; 〜ついでに stresses the opportunity or convenience.

meaning: 1) While a state lasts (after which it will be hard to do): "while ..., before ... (changes)"; 2) during an ongoing action, a change happens without one noticing: "in the course of ..., before you know it".
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている form / nai-form + うちに; i-adjective + うちに; na-adjective + な + うちに; noun + の + うちに
usage: "While" use: the first clause is a state that will end or change, and the second is usually a deliberate action by the speaker: 「若いうちに」, 「熱いうちに」, 「暗くならないうちに」.
"Without noticing" use: the first clause is usually 〜ている／〜ているうちに, and the second a change that happens naturally: 「話しているうちに、仲良くなった」.
The negative 〜ないうちに is close to 〜まえに, but stresses "hurry and do it before that happens".
「〜うちは」 means "as long as ... (it's fine)", with a contrastive nuance: 「若いうちは何でもできる」.
Distinguish it from 「うち」 meaning "home, us": in 「友達がうちに来た」, うち means "my house".
scenarios: Urging someone to do something while they can (conversation): 「冷めないうちに、どうぞ召し上がってください。」
Life advice and reflections: 「若いうちに、いろいろな国へ行ったほうがいい。」
Describing an unnoticed change (novels, essays): 「本を読んでいるうちに、眠ってしまった。」
Reminders about weather or time: 「暗くならないうちに帰りましょう。」
etymology: うち is written 「内」, originally meaning "inside, interior"; it is the same word as 「うち（家・内）」 meaning "home". Applied to time, it means "within a certain time span", giving the use "during ... (while it lasts)"; and since a change happens in the middle of an ongoing process, it further developed the "without noticing" use.
examples: Please eat it while it's warm.
Let's hurry home before it starts raining.
While watching Japanese dramas, my Japanese got better.
Let's finish our homework while we can.

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: Simply expresses time order (before ...); 〜ないうちに stresses "hurry before an unfavorable situation arises".

similar.title: 〜間に
similar.explanation: 「〜間に」 means a one-time event happens within a clearly defined period, an objective description; 〜うちに carries the sense of "seizing the chance" or "before you know it".

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: Two actions at the same time with the same subject; 〜ているうちに means some other change arises during the process.

similar.title: 〜ついでに
similar.explanation: Doing something on the side by taking an opportunity, focusing on the "opportunity"; 〜うちに focuses on the "time span".

meaning: 1) The cause of a good result, with gratitude: "thanks to ..."; 2) ironic use with a bad result, expressing complaint or sarcasm: "thanks to ... (not!)", "all because of ...".
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + おかげで; na-adjective + な + おかげで; noun + の + おかげで (sentence-final: 〜おかげだ)
usage: The second clause is generally a good result, and it expresses thanks to the person or thing in the first clause.
Sentence-final form: 「〜のおかげだ／〜のおかげです」: 「合格できたのは先生のおかげです。」
「おかげさまで」 is a set greeting used in reply to someone asking after you: 「おかげさまで、元気です」 (I'm well, thank you).
With bad results it becomes sarcastic: 「君が遅れたおかげで、電車に乗り遅れたよ」.
In polite contexts it can also be written 「お陰で」 or 「お蔭で」.
scenarios: Thanking someone who helped you (conversation, letters): 「先生のおかげで、試験に合格できました。」
Exchanging greetings: 「お元気ですか。」「おかげさまで。」
Describing something that made life easier: 「新しい駅ができたおかげで、通勤が楽になった。」
Joking complaints between friends: 「お前が騒いだおかげで、怒られたじゃないか。」
etymology: 「おかげ」 is written 「御陰・御蔭」, made of the honorific prefix 「お（御）」 + 「陰・蔭（かげ）」 (shade), originally referring to the sheltering protection of gods and buddhas, later extended to favors and help given by others. 「おかげさまで」 thus means "thanks to (you and the gods)". The お蔭参り pilgrimages to Ise Shrine, popular in the Edo period, also reflect this religious origin.
examples: Thanks to my teacher, I passed the Japanese Language Proficiency Test.
Thanks to the medicine I took, my fever went down.
It's all thanks to everyone's help.
Thanks to you, I'm doing well.

similar.title: 〜せいで
similar.explanation: Expresses the cause of a bad result, with blame; 〜おかげで is for good results and includes gratitude. The two form an opposite pair.

similar.title: 〜ために (cause)
similar.explanation: States a cause neutrally, with neither thanks nor blame; more written.

similar.title: 〜から・〜ので
similar.explanation: General expressions of cause and reason without emotional coloring; they can be followed by requests, commands, etc.

meaning: 1) The cause of a bad result, or who is to blame: "because of ..., all due to ..."; 2) 〜せいか: an uncertain cause, "perhaps because ..."; 3) 〜のせいにする: to blame something on ....
connection: Plain form of verbs / i-adjectives + せいで; na-adjective + な + せいで; noun + の + せいで (sentence-final: 〜せいだ)
usage: The second clause is a bad or troublesome result, and the first is the cause being blamed, with a tone of complaint or reproach.
Sentence-final form: 「〜のせいだ」: 「失敗したのは私のせいです」 (the failure is my fault).
「〜せいか」 expresses the speaker's vague guess at a cause, and the result isn't necessarily bad: 「年のせいか、疲れやすい」.
「人のせいにする」 means shifting the blame: 「自分の失敗を人のせいにしてはいけない。」
It is generally written in kana; the kanji spelling is rarely used today.
scenarios: Complaining about the cause of a problem (conversation): 「台風のせいで、旅行が中止になった。」
Admitting your responsibility and apologizing: 「私のせいで、ご迷惑をおかけしました。」
Guessing the cause of how you feel: 「寝不足のせいか、頭が痛い。」
Criticizing someone for shifting blame: 「人のせいにするな。」
etymology: 「せい」 is traditionally written with two kanji meaning roughly "what is done". One theory traces it to the Sino-Japanese word しょい ("that which someone has done"), whose reading changed to せい; it originally meant "what (someone) did, the result they caused", and extended to "reason, cause, blame". Because opinions on its origin differ, it is mostly written in kana today.
examples: Because of the rain, the game was canceled.
Because I played games until late at night, I couldn't get up in the morning.
Maybe it's my age, but I get tired easily lately.
You shouldn't blame others for your own failures.
It's my fault that we lost.

similar.title: 〜おかげで
similar.explanation: Used for good results with gratitude, the opposite of 〜せいで; but おかげで used with a bad result becomes sarcastic.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: States a cause objectively and in a written style, without blame.

similar.title: 〜ために (cause)
similar.explanation: States a cause neutrally; 〜せいで carries a clear negative evaluation and sense of blame.

meaning: Indicates an evaluation or judgment from the standpoint of a person or organization: "for ..., to ..., as far as ... is concerned".
connection: Noun + にとって／にとっては／にとっても／にとっての + noun
usage: The second clause is usually evaluative: 大切だ, 難しい, ありがたい, 問題だ, 必要だ, etc., rather than a concrete action.
It usually follows a subject that can "experience" something, such as people, organizations, or living things: 「私にとって」, 「会社にとって」, 「植物にとって」.
「にとっては」 has a contrastive nuance (for ..., at least), and 「にとっても」 means "for ... too".
To modify a noun use 「にとっての + noun」: 「私にとっての幸せ」.
It can't be followed by words expressing attitudes or actions: ×「先生にとって親切だ」 → ○「先生に対して親切だ」.
scenarios: Expressing personal values or feelings (essays, speeches): 「私にとって、家族は一番大切なものです。」
Discussing the impact on a group (reports, papers): 「この法律は中小企業にとって大きな負担になる。」
Explaining how difficult something is, e.g. that honorific language is hard 「外国人にとって」 (for foreigners).
etymology: Made of the case particle 「に」, marking the target, and 「取って」, the te-form of the verb 「取る」 (to take); the old form 「に取りて」 became 「にとって」 through a geminate sound change. Literally "taking it with regard to ...", i.e. "viewed from the standpoint of ...". It is now fully grammaticalized and almost always written in kana.
examples: To me, this photo is a treasure.
For international students, finding an apartment is hard.
This decision is a big problem for the company as well.
What does happiness mean for a child?

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: Marks the target of an attitude or action (toward ...), followed by 親切だ, 反対する, etc.; 〜にとって is followed by evaluations.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: Expresses identity or capacity (as ...); 〜にとって expresses the standpoint of an evaluation (for ...). 「親として心配だ」 focuses on worrying in one's capacity as a parent; 「親にとって心配だ」 focuses on it being a worry for parents.

similar.title: 〜にしたら・〜にすれば
similar.explanation: Mean "imagining it from ...'s point of view", mostly used to guess others' feelings: 「親にしたら心配だろう」; 〜にとって is more objective.
